The physical layer is of course not of zero thickness: Problem D2 works out that in sea-level air it is a few mean free paths, about $2\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{cm}$, which is $2\times10^{8}$ times thinner than the Trinity fireball was one millisecond after detonation.

In 1950 Taylor published twenty-five radii against twenty-five times, read off that film, and compared them with the prediction he had made nine years before seeing it. §5 repeats the comparison from his own table, and finds two things: the exponent is confirmed to better than two and a half per cent over a factor of 620 in time, and the model that produced the exponent is refuted by the residuals from the very same fit.

The module then leaves the laboratory twice. §6 uses a shock that a spacecraft flew through and measured from inside — Voyager 2 at the solar-wind termination shock in 2007, with Neptune's bow shock from the same instrument eighteen years earlier as a control.

The control confirms the compression ceiling exactly; the termination shock refutes the single-fluid closure this book has used since Module 2, and the way it fails is precisely the way Module 1 said a collisionless plasma would fail. §7 then follows a supernova remnant from the moment the Sedov solution becomes valid to the moment it stops being valid, and §8 pays a debt: Module 7 closed by recording that its Rayleigh–Taylor half had no astronomical check anywhere in Modules 1–10.

Polytropic with the same $\gamma$ on both sides is the assumption §5 finds broken at Trinity, where dissociation, vibration and radiation all act behind the front and Taylor argues — with evidence, and not quite successfully — that they cancel.

It required each equation to be a divergence, which is why the conservation forms were taken and not the convective ones: $\partial_t(\rho v)$ written as $\rho[\partial_t v + (v\cdot\nabla)v]$ is not a divergence and cannot be integrated across a discontinuity.

It required the endpoints to lie in gas with no gradients, which is the whole working content of "the thickness is negligible": the layer must be thin enough that uniform gas is reached on both sides before anything else in the problem has changed.
And it required every source to be a bounded volume source, so a layer that radiates away a finite amount of energy per unit area — a surface loss, not a bounded volume loss — breaks (2.4).

What the proof did not use is any value of $\sigma_{nn}$, of $q_n$ or of the thickness, any equation of state inside the layer, or any assumption that the gas in there is in local thermodynamic equilibrium.

Problem D2 shows that the trade is a good one in air and a very bad one at the termination shock, where the layer is $10^5$ to $10^6$ times thinner than a collisional mean free path and the phrase "local thermodynamic equilibrium" has no referent at all.

Compression is bounded because the gas that piles up behind the front pushes back, and past a certain density no increase in the ram pressure can make it denser; heating is unbounded because the kinetic energy that has to go somewhere goes into internal energy, and internal energy has no ceiling.

That single sentence explains why supernova remnants shine in X-rays rather than looking like dense shells, and why §7 can speak of $10^8\ \mathrm{K}$ gas at a density of a few particles per cubic centimetre.

What happens instead is a rarefaction fan : an expansion spreads out into a continuous region whose width grows with time, because each characteristic in it travels at its own speed and the faster ones run ahead.

A $10\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ flow — a very ordinary speed in the interstellar medium, far below anything a supernova produces — is then at $\mathcal{M} = 52.9$ and compresses the gas by a factor $2802$.

Put the same speed through an adiabatic shock and it is at $M_1 = \mathcal{M}/\sqrt\gamma = 41.0$, because the adiabatic sound speed in the same gas is $\sqrt\gamma\,c_T = 0.244\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$, and it compresses by $3.993$.

Voyager 2's plasma experiment recorded a decrease in solar-wind speed from about 9 June 2007, culminating in several crossings of the solar-wind termination shock at a heliocentric radius of 84 AU between 30 August and 1 September 2007.

From the figure caption comparing the two crossings, read directly: at Neptune's bow shock the solar-wind speed fell by a factor of four and the density increased by a factor of four, while the temperature increased by a factor of 100.

That the density jump and the speed drop are the same number is mass conservation, (2.2), holding to the precision of the read — provided the bow shock is standing in the frame the speeds were measured in, which a planetary bow shock does to that precision, because (2.2) is a statement in the rest frame of the surface and the speeds are measured in the spacecraft's.

The authors state the consequence plainly: if all the flow energy were transferred to the thermal ions, as happens at planetary bow shocks, the heliosheath temperature would be $10^6$ K, whereas the observed temperature is $10^5$ K.

The energy per proton falls by 80 per cent across the shock, and it goes to pickup ions — hot protons created when neutral interstellar atoms are ionised inside the heliosphere — rather than to the thermal plasma.

This module does the thing neither of them did: it takes the steady spherical flow seriously as an equation to be solved, discovers that the equation has a singular point, and finds that almost everything worth knowing about stellar winds and about accretion onto compact objects follows from the behaviour of solutions near that point.

What is left is one ordinary differential equation for the speed $v(r)$, and that equation contains no information about which way the gas is going: $v$ enters it through $v^2$ and through $\mathrm{d}\ln v/\mathrm{d}\ln r$, and a solution with $v \gt 0$ everywhere maps onto a solution with $v \lt 0$ everywhere.

The solution that satisfies it is the only one that starts subsonic at a stellar surface and ends supersonic at infinity — and a wind that does not end supersonic decelerates as $v \propto r^{-2}$, which is a qualitatively different object with a qualitatively different signature in the data. §7 uses exactly that: the sign of a measured velocity exponent separates the two, with no fitting.

In one dimension, with $U = (\rho, \rho u, E)$ the densities of mass, momentum and total energy and $F(U) = (\rho u, \rho u^{2} + P, u(E + P))$ their fluxes, they read $\partial_t U + \partial_x F(U) = 0$, where $E = P/(\gamma-1) + \rho u^{2}/2$ for an ideal gas.

That code updates $U_iV_i$, with $V_i$ the cell volume, through faces of area $r^{2}$, and the same telescoping conserves its total mass and energy; its momentum equation has a geometric source, and radial momentum is not conserved in spherical symmetry.

The upwind scheme takes the flux from the cell the flow comes from, $F_{i+1/2} = a u_i$, so (1.1) becomes $$ u_i^{n+1} = u_i^n - C\,(u_i^n - u_{i-1}^n), \qquad C = \frac{a\Delta t}{\Delta x}. \tag{2.1}$$ The forward-time centred-space scheme (FTCS) takes the average of the two neighbours, $F_{i+1/2} = a(u_i + u_{i+1})/2$, and gives $u_i^{n+1} = u_i^n - \tfrac{C}{2}(u_{i+1}^n - u_{i-1}^n)$.
At $C = 1$ the upwind scheme is $u_i^{n+1} = u_{i-1}^n$: it moves the data exactly one cell per step, which is the exact solution, and (2.3) gives $|G| = 1$ for every mode.

The run applies Godunov's method at $C_{\rm CFL} = 0.9$ on $N = 100$ to $6400$ cells, measures the $L_1$ error of the density, $\sum_i|\rho_i - \rho_{\rm exact}(x_i)|\Delta x$, and splits it at the midpoints between the waves ($x = 0.585718$ and $0.767961$) into the fan, the contact and the shock.

The Riemann problem between two cells with the same $P$ and $u$ and different $\rho$ has as its solution the contact alone, moving at $u^{*}$, so Godunov's flux of mass there is exactly $\rho_i u^{*}$: the upwind flux.
The density across the contact is therefore advected by (2.1) at the Courant number $C_{\rm c} = u^{*}\Delta t/\Delta x$, which the run records step by step (its mean is $0.3810$ at $N = 6400$).

Each step replaces $d_i$ by the weighted average $(1 - C_{\rm c})d_i + C_{\rm c}d_{i-1}$, so for $0 \le C_{\rm c} \le 1$ the spike stays non-negative and Proposition 5 applies at every step: the total stays $\Delta\rho_{\rm c}$, and the variance grows to $\sigma^{2} = \sum_n C_{\rm c}(1 - C_{\rm c})\Delta x^{2}$.

After many steps the sum of these independent two-point moves has a Gaussian profile, by the central limit theorem, whose conditions hold because each move is at most one cell and the variances sum without limit.

A step of height $\Delta\rho_{\rm c}$ smoothed by a Gaussian of width $\sigma$ has an $L_1$ error $2\Delta\rho_{\rm c}\int_0^\infty[1 - \Phi(y/\sigma)]\,\mathrm{d}y$, with $\Phi$ the standard normal distribution function, which is $$ E_{\rm c} \;=\; \Delta\rho_{\rm c}\,\sigma\left(\frac{2}{\pi}\right)^{1/2}, \qquad \sigma \propto \Delta x^{1/2}. \tag{5.1}$$ With $\Delta\rho_{\rm c} = 0.160746$ this has no free parameter.
The excess falls with $N$ faster than $E_{\rm c}$ does: it is $1.1293 - 1$ of $E_{\rm c}$ at $N = 100$ and $1.0659 - 1$ at $N = 6400$, and the ratio falls at every doubling.

Two readers went through Modules 1 to 13 and classified every number that a module compares against or takes as an input: (a) the output of a numerical simulation; (b) a numerical model built by solving equations on a computer, such as the BS05 solar model table or the ATLAS9 model atmosphere; (c) an ordinary differential equation with no closed form, integrated numerically, by this book's own script or, in 3 of the 30 rows, by a published integration (Chandrasekhar's in Module 3, Kandori's in Module 5), such as Lane–Emden, Bonnor–Ebert, Sedov, or the critical solutions of Bondi and Parker.

The closed-form results that carry the book are the other column: the mean free paths of Module 1 , the jump conditions and the $2/5$ exponent of Module 8 , Kolmogorov's $5/3$ and $4/5$ in Module 10 , the Eddington limit of Module 13 .

The module captures the three properties of a numerical scheme that decide whether its output can be trusted as a solution of the equations of this book: stability (the Courant condition), the equation it actually solves (the numerical viscosity), and its convergence on the discontinuities that astrophysical flows contain.

Of the debts the shipped pages and the plan printed against this module, six are paid: the Courant condition that Module 10 Proposition 4 used, by Propositions 2 and 3; which problem a code solves ( module10.html:285 , :918 ), by Propositions 4 and 5 and §10 ; how a collapse is followed ( module05.html:767 ), by §9 ; Riemann solvers, by §4 and §5 ; grid against SPH, by §7 and §8 ; and the census, by §11 .

phrase_occurrences.text: The second half of that definition is not a technicality, and it is where most errors of judgement enter. The Knudsen number is a property of the question, not of the gas. The photospheric gas of §4.1 has one mean free path, 66 µm, but two Knudsen numbers. Measured against the solar radius it is $9.6\times10^{-14}$; measured against the pressure scale height of about 150 km, which is the scale on which convection organises itself and therefore the scale a model of granulation must resolve, it is $4.4\times10^{-10}$. Both are minute, so here the distinction changes nothing. In §7 we meet a case where it changes everything.

Two consequences are worth stating plainly. First, the density-independence of viscosity is not an artefact of the plasma case: it is Maxwell's result for any gas. He derived it in 1860, did not believe the experiments then available, and tested it himself with Katherine Maxwell in 1865–66, finding the viscosity of air constant over a wide range of pressure. Second, the $T^{5/2}$ law makes hot plasma a very good conductor of heat. Raising the temperature from $10^6$ to $10^8$ K raises $\kappa$ by $(100)^{5/2}=10^5$ from the power alone, or by $8.8\times10^{4}$ once the accompanying rise in $\ln\Lambda$ from 32.5 to 37.1 is included. This is why unsuppressed thermal conduction would erase the temperature structure observed in cluster cores within a fraction of the cluster's age, and it is the reason the question of what suppresses it is a live one. We return to it in Module 12, where magnetic fields provide the answer.

At 1 AU the solar wind has $\mathrm{Kn}\approx1.9$. By the hierarchy of §6 there should be no fluid description of it at all, and the situation is more extreme than $\mathrm{Kn}\approx2$ on its own suggests. Take the radial scalings of problem K1 , under which $\lambda(r) = 1.94\,r^{-2/3}$ AU with $r$ measured in AU, and integrate the collision rate along the outflow. The expected number of Coulomb collisions a proton suffers between the corona and Earth's orbit is $$ \int_0^{1}\frac{dr}{\lambda(r)} \;=\; \frac{1}{1.94}\int_0^1 r^{2/3}\,dr \;=\; \frac{3}{5\times1.94} \;=\; 0.31. $$ Fewer than one proton in three arriving at Earth has collided even once since it left the Sun. And yet magnetohydrodynamic models of the solar wind reproduce its large-scale structure — the spiral field, the stream interaction regions, the propagation of coronal mass ejections — with considerable success. Something other than collisions is confining the particles.

Nothing about the gas changed; $L$ changed. The quoted figure uses $L=100$ pc, appropriate to a large cloud complex. The mean free path is 134 AU, so any structure whose interesting scale approaches that length has a Knudsen number of order unity. A concrete example is the transition layer at the edge of a cold neutral cloud, across which temperature falls from 8000 K to under 100 K; such interfaces are observed to be thin, and a model that must resolve a 100 AU interface has $\mathrm{Kn}\sim1$ and no fluid description of the interface itself. The bulk flow around the cloud remains perfectly fluid. The correct statement is that the Euler equations hold for interstellar problems whose resolution requirement exceeds a few thousand AU.

It measures a Knudsen number, or equivalently places a lower bound on a mean free path. In the collision the gas, which has $\mathrm{Kn}\ll1$, behaved as a fluid: it shocked, dissipated kinetic energy and was left behind between the two subclusters. The galaxies and the lensing mass, having $\mathrm{Kn}\gg1$, passed through each other without interacting. The separation between the two components is therefore a direct measure of the difference in their collisionality, and converting the observed offset into a limit gives $\sigma/m \lt 0.7\ \mathrm{cm^2\,g^{-1}}$ (Randall et al. 2008), hence $\lambda\ge23$ Mpc and $\mathrm{Kn}\ge23$.

Two readings. First, $\mathrm{Kn}$ decreases outward here, and the crossing lies just outside Earth's orbit: the wind at 1 AU is already at $\mathrm{Kn}=1.9$, so on this model the fluid description fails everywhere inside about 1.5 AU and recovers beyond it. That is an artefact worth naming — it follows from assuming $L=r$, which makes the available scale grow faster than the mean free path shrinks. Judged instead against a fixed structure, such as the 0.01 AU thickness of a stream interaction region, the wind is collisionless throughout. Second, the exponent $-5/3$ is shallow, so the crossing radius is insensitive to the inputs: doubling $\lambda(1)$ moves it only to 2.3 AU. The conclusion that the solar wind is not collisional at scales a spacecraft can resolve is robust; the precise crossing radius is not, and adiabatic cooling is itself a poor model, since the observed wind cools more slowly than $r^{-4/3}$ because it is heated in transit.

On the resolution question the answer is the opposite of comfortable. At $r=1.73$ Mpc the mean free path is $\lambda = 0.575\times302 = 173$ kpc — seventeen times larger than the 10 kpc cell. The simulation therefore resolves, in detail, a range of scales on which the gas has no fluid description at all, and it solves the Euler equations on every one of them. Its cells at that radius are not small parcels of fluid; they are boxes containing particles that will not collide before they have crossed many boxes. Refining the mesh makes this worse, not better. Nothing is wrong with the arithmetic in such a simulation; what is wrong is the claim that its resolved structure in the outskirts represents gas dynamics.

Taking moments of the Boltzmann equation: how six dimensions become four, why the procedure never closes on its own, and a measured flow that tests the first equation to two per cent while breaking the third by forty.
10. The check: does a measured flow obey these equations?

The route is as follows. §2 defines the moments and the fields they produce. §3 proves that exactly five of them obey exact equations, and explains why there are five and not six. §4 derives the general moment equation and exhibits the gap. §5 to §8 work out the three cases: mass, momentum and energy. §9 closes the system and states what licence we have to do so. §10 takes the first of the resulting equations to a measured astronomical flow and checks it.

First, no approximation was made. Equation (5.1) contains no closure assumption, no expansion in the Knudsen number, and no appeal to a Maxwellian. It is a consequence of counting particles and of the fact that collisions do not create or destroy them. A collisionless plasma obeys it; so does a galaxy, with "density" meaning the mass density of stars. This is why §10 can use it as a sharp test: a measured departure from (5.1) would mean the measurement is wrong, or that mass is entering the flow from outside it, and nothing else.
10. The check: does a measured flow obey these equations?

The solar wind supplies the test. It is the only astrophysical flow whose density and speed have been measured in situ at many heliocentric distances by instruments flying through it, so the radial dependence is a measurement rather than an inference.

Equation (10.2) is the ideal test object. It contains no coefficient to be fitted, no cross-section, no efficiency factor and no calibration. Two exponents are measured independently and their difference is predicted to be an integer.

One step in the argument has to be made explicit before the comparison means anything, because it is the only place where an extra assumption enters. Proposition 13 governs a single steady stream. The fitted exponents describe the mean, or the median, of a distribution of measurements at each radius, and the solar wind at any radius is a mixture of streams — the slow wind dense and the fast wind tenuous, so that $n$ and $v$ are anticorrelated across the sample. Continuity constrains the mean of the product, $\langle nv\rangle$, while the table supplies the exponents of $\langle n\rangle$ and $\langle v\rangle$ separately. The two agree if the mixture is radially self-similar over the observed range: each stream obeying the same pair of exponents, and the relative weights of the streams not changing with distance. Under that condition the mixture inherits the exponents of its components, and $\alpha-\beta=2$ carries across to the fitted quantities.

The continuity test. Upper panel: the measured exponent difference $\alpha-\beta$ for the mean and median Helios fits, with the formal fit uncertainty as the thick bar and the larger year-to-year scatter of the exponents as the pale bar, against the value $2$ that Proposition 13 requires exactly. Both fits agree with the prediction within one standard deviation and they bracket it. Lower panel: the same fits expressed as the mass flux $4\pi r^2\rho v$, divided by its value at 1 AU. A flow obeying (10.1) would trace the flat line. The mean fit drifts upward by $4.9$ per cent across the observed range and the median fit downward by $4.2$ per cent, both inside the $\pm 5$ per cent band. The residual is a measurement of how far the real wind departs from being steady and spherical, not of any failure of the equation.

This second check is weaker than the first and the difference is worth naming, because it is the difference between two kinds of evidence. Equation (10.2) compares a measured exponent with an exact integer that the equation predicts and nothing else could have produced. Equation (10.3) compares one number against another number of the same kind, derived from overlapping data; agreement confirms that neither calculation contains a gross error, but it does not test the equation, because any flux at all could have been accommodated by a different $\dot M$. Treat (10.3) as a calibration, and (10.2) as the result.
The mean fits have $\alpha = 2.010$, so (10.4) predicts a temperature exponent of $-1.340$. The measured mean exponent is $-0.792\pm0.028$.

That also limits what the measurement can be said to show. Equation (8.2) was reduced to the adiabatic form (8.3) by dropping three separate things: the viscous heating $\sigma_{ij}\partial_ju_i$, the conduction term $-\nabla\cdot\mathbf{q}$, and any external heating source, which (8.2) does not contain at all. A single measured temperature exponent constrains their sum and cannot separate them. At $\mathrm{Kn}\approx2$ the heat flux is certainly not small, so conduction alone could in principle account for part of the shortfall. The attribution of the remainder to in-situ turbulent heating is the field's, not this module's, and as noted above it is unverified here. What is established by these data is narrower and still worth having: the adiabatic closure is excluded, at $19.6\sigma$ for the mean fits.

One structural limitation is worth separating from the list, because no later module repairs it. The moment hierarchy of Fig. 1 does not close, and there is no choice of closure that is correct in general. Chapman–Enskog produces an asymptotic expansion in $\mathrm{Kn}$, and an asymptotic expansion is not a convergent one: truncating at second order gives the Burnett equations, which are not uniformly better than Navier–Stokes and can be unstable. Where $\mathrm{Kn}$ is of order unity there is no fluid model at all, only the Boltzmann equation itself or a direct simulation of particles. The solar wind sits there, and the reason the fluid picture survives in it is not that the expansion converges but that a magnetic field supplies a shorter transverse length scale, as Module 1 §8.1 set out.

Note the direction of this argument. The small imbalance is not assumed in order to simplify the equations. It is forced by the observed luminosity. By (2.5), an imbalance larger than about $10^{-24}$ means contraction on a timescale $t$ shorter than $t_{\rm KH}$. Such a contraction releases gravitational energy of order $GM^2/R$ in time $t$, a power $GM^2/(Rt)$ larger than $L$ by the factor $t_{\rm KH}/t$ from (1.2). By the virial argument of §8 , half of that energy must leave the star, and the observed luminosity does not carry it. Setting $\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{0}$ in (2.1) discards a term of that relative size.
Inverting (4.2) turns a measured lapse rate $\Gamma \equiv |dT/dz|$ into a polytropic index, $n = \mu m_u g/(k_B\Gamma) - 1$. Two lapse rates of the Earth's atmosphere are worth converting.

Two stability criteria are derived in this module, and both can be applied to these numbers. The first, Jeans's criterion, treats the cloud as a piece of a uniform medium. It gives a critical mass of $2.97\,M_\odot$, larger than the cloud's mass, so it calls the cloud stable. The second, the Bonnor–Ebert criterion, treats the cloud as a pressure-bounded isothermal sphere and uses the shape of its density profile. The measured shape parameter is $\xi_{\max} = 6.9\pm0.2$ against a critical value of $6.4508$, so it calls the cloud unstable.

Perturbations with $\lambda\gt\lambda_J$ grow, and those with $\lambda\lt\lambda_J$ oscillate. The Jeans mass is a convention, not a derived threshold: (3.1) is a statement about plane waves, and the choice of a sphere of diameter $\lambda_J$ is one of several in use. A cube of side $\lambda_J$ gives a mass larger by $6/\pi = 1.9099$. The factor matters in §7.2 , where the Jeans mass is compared with a measured mass, and it is stated there.

For a fixed temperature, a Bonnor–Ebert sphere has two parameters, $\rho_c$ and $\xi_{\max}$. Its shape, the profile $\rho/\rho_c$ against $r/R$, depends only on $\xi_{\max}$. This is what makes the model testable against a single measured profile: one number fixes the shape.

What the fit determines. The profile fixes the shape, $\xi_{\max}$, but not the scale. Kandori et al. (2005, section 4.2.2) show, crediting Lai et al. (2003), that substituting $R\propto d$ and $\rho_c\propto d^{-1}$ for a cloud at distance $d$ into the definition of $\xi_{\max}$ gives $T/d = \text{constant}$. The same fitted shape is therefore consistent with a line of temperature-distance pairs. The second Barnard 68 line of Table 5, from Hotzel, Harju & Juvela (2002), takes the measured temperature $10\pm1.2$ K and reads $d = 85$ pc, $R = 0.85\times10^{4}$ AU and $M = 0.90\,M_\odot$. At fixed $\xi_{\max}$ the mass scales as $c_s^2R\propto Td$, which predicts a mass ratio of $2.3529$ between the two lines; the table gives $2.3333$, a ratio of $0.9917$.

What this refutes must be stated precisely. It does not refute hydrostatic equilibrium, the isothermal closure or the fits, because these are the instrument by which $\xi_{\max}$ was measured. It refutes the reading that these clouds are long-lived stable equilibria of the kind the fits describe. How fast an unstable sphere departs is not computed here. The rate is $(G\rho_c)^{1/2}$ times a function of $\xi_{\max}$ that passes through zero at $\xi_{\rm crit}$, where the sequence changes stability, so a sphere just above the critical point, as Barnard 68 is at $\xi_{\max}/\xi_{\rm crit} = 1.0696$, can depart much more slowly than the free-fall time, $1.70\times10^{5}$ yr at its mean density.

The second is the density slope, which Nielbock et al. derive from the same radiative-transfer model. Their abstract gives $n_{\rm H}\propto r^{-3.5}$ outside the inner plateau. §5 showed that the local slope $-d\ln\rho/d\ln r$ of an isothermal sphere does not exceed $2.5176$ on the integrated range, for any $\xi_{\max}$. The measured slope is $1.390$ times that ceiling.

A comparison at matched radius is sharper. Their adopted profile is $n_{\rm H}(r) = \Delta n/[1 + (r/r_0)^2]^{\eta/2} + n_{\rm out}$ with $r_0 = 35''$, $\eta = 4.0$, $n_0 = \Delta n + n_{\rm out} = 3.4\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ and $n_{\rm out} = 4\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ (their equation 8 and adopted values). The Bonnor–Ebert sphere of Alves et al. has $\xi_{\max} = 6.9$ at $100''$, so its local slope at angular radius $\theta$ is $\xi\psi'$ at $\xi = 6.9\,\theta/100''$. Both profiles are functions of angle, so neither distance enters. Fig. 4 compares them. The measured slope exceeds the isothermal ceiling for $\theta\gt46.2''$, that is over the outer $53.8$ per cent of the fitted radius. At $60''$ it is $2.9309$ against $2.0219$ for the fitted sphere; at $100''$ it is $3.2428$ against $2.4660$, a ratio of $1.315$.

What is refuted is the conjunction of four assumptions for the outer half of Barnard 68: static, spherical, isothermal and self-gravitating. The fluid equations are not refuted. The slope test alone does not say which assumption fails. A gas whose temperature rises outward, as the dust temperature does here, has a pressure that falls more slowly than its density, so it can hold a steeper density profile in hydrostatic balance; departure from spherical symmetry and a non-static outer layer are the other candidates, and this module separates none of them. Hydrostatic balance is not stability. A stratified fluid can fail in two independent ways: buoyancy can stop restoring a displaced parcel, which is convection, and cooling can run away under compression, which is thermal instability. The Schwarzschild and Ledoux criteria, the collapse of the adiabatic gradient in an ionisation zone, mixing-length theory and its price, then Field's criterion and the two-phase interstellar medium. Two checks against measured data: mixing-length theory against solar granulation, and the predicted two-phase pressure window against 89 measured lines of sight.

The second is cooling. Compress a parcel of interstellar gas a little, at the pressure of its surroundings. If the compression makes it radiate away energy faster than it gains it, the parcel cools, and at fixed pressure a cooler parcel is denser, so it contracts further. No gravity is involved at all. §8 derives Field's criterion for that runaway, §9 shows that it carves the interstellar medium into two stable phases separated by a narrow band of pressures, and §10 compares the predicted band with 89 measured sight lines. That comparison is the anchor of this module, and it confirms one prediction and refutes another from the same measurement.

The content of that confirmation is that a factor-$2.5$ window exists at all, and sits where it does. Neither of its edges was fitted to a pressure value. Wolfire et al. computed $P_{\min}$ and $P_{\max}$ from grain photoelectric heating and [C II]/[O I] cooling, with gas-phase carbon and oxygen abundances fixed by independent Hubble absorption-line studies and a PAH abundance fixed by ISO infrared emission data. One heating parameter, $\varphi_{\rm PAH} = 0.5$, was calibrated to an observed C I/C II column-density ratio; Wolfire's own detailed working credits that ratio to the C I and H I data compiled by Welty & Hobbs (2001), although an earlier passage cites Jenkins & Tripp (2001) alongside it. Jenkins & Tripp (2001) is the predecessor of, and distinct from, the 2011 pressure measurement compared here.

What mitigates that must be stated as precisely as the defect, and it is stronger than one row. Wolfire et al. disfavour every non-standard variant, on evidence that is not a pressure. Their four-item summary reads, in their order: "Low $\varphi_{\rm PAH}$" models poorly match the C I*/C$_{\rm tot}$ ratio and the C$^+$ cooling rate, with values lower than observed; "High $\varphi_{\rm PAH}$" models produce temperatures and C I/C II ratios higher than observed; "Low PAH" — Table 4's "Low $n_{\rm PAH}/n$" — gives low C I*/C$_{\rm tot}$ ratios and C$^+$ cooling rate; "Low $G_0$" gives low C I*/C$_{\rm tot}$ and high C I/C II. Separately, they write that only "High $\varphi_{\rm PAH}$" and "Low $G_0$" "can be safely ruled out by the required C I/C II ratio".

The two tiers must be kept apart. Two rows are ruled out in those words. Two more, including the one that breaks the confirmation, are called a worse fit on two independent diagnostics without being ruled out. The only variant Wolfire et al. do not argue against is the standard one, and the standard one contains the measured median.

One number is stable across all five variants: the measured median exceeds every predicted average pressure, from $1.033$ times the "High $\varphi_{\rm PAH}$" value to $1.713$ times the "Low $\varphi_{\rm PAH}$" one. The measurement runs high against the central model value whatever the parameters. Only the window verdict moves.
10.3 Refuted: a static two-phase medium cannot put cold gas below $P_{\min}$

Below $P_{\min}$ the equilibrium curve has no cold branch: by Proposition 8 the only equilibrium state at such a pressure is the warm one. A strict, static two-phase medium therefore allows none of the cold neutral medium to sit below $P_{\min}$. Jenkins & Tripp measured the cold medium, and they report in their section 10.1.2 that $29$ per cent of it is there.

The two halves of the module are tested differently, and the difference is worth stating at the start. The Rayleigh–Taylor half is checked against a laboratory measurement — a laser-driven experiment at the National Ignition Facility — and that is the only place in this module where a standard deviation exists. The Kelvin–Helmholtz half is checked against a solar observation which quotes every input to one significant figure and gives no uncertainty at all. §9 says so in its first paragraph, and then shows what such an observation can still be made to yield: not a confirmation, but a bound on a magnetic field that nobody measured.

Two things follow from Definition 3 alone and are worth having before any algebra. First, $\sigma$ has dimensions of inverse time, so $1/\sigma$ is an e-folding time and a growth is only meaningful against some other clock — the age of a supernova remnant, the duration of an observation. Second, because $\sigma$ will turn out to depend on $k$, the interface does not simply "go unstable": it goes unstable at some wavelengths and not at others, and the one that grows fastest is what an experiment or an image shows.

A simulation of this problem has no converged answer. The growth rate rises as $\sqrt{k}$, so whatever the smallest resolved scale is, that is the scale that goes unstable first, and refining the grid changes the answer rather than improving it. The cut-off must come from somewhere the ideal equations do not contain: from viscosity, as in (4.4); from a finite interface thickness, which §9 shows is the realistic case for an astrophysical boundary; or from the magnetic tension term of (3.1), which Module 12 takes up. What Proposition 4 establishes is that something must supply it, and that the ideal fluid model of Modules 2–11 does not.

The module then leaves the laboratory twice. §6 uses a shock that a spacecraft flew through and measured from inside — Voyager 2 at the solar-wind termination shock in 2007, with Neptune's bow shock from the same instrument eighteen years earlier as a control. 6.2 REFUTED: the closure, not the conservation laws

At the termination shock the same instrument found the temperature increasing by a factor of only ten and the density by only two. The authors state the consequence plainly: if all the flow energy were transferred to the thermal ions, as happens at planetary bow shocks, the heliosheath temperature would be $10^6$ K, whereas the observed temperature is $10^5$ K.

The authors' explanation is what makes this a refutation of a specific hypothesis rather than a puzzle. The energy per proton falls by 80 per cent across the shock, and it goes to pickup ions — hot protons created when neutral interstellar atoms are ionised inside the heliosphere — rather than to the thermal plasma. A single-fluid ideal gas has nowhere to put that energy, so it predicts a hot thermal population that is not there. And Module 1 has already said why this is possible: the solar wind at 84 AU is collisionless, so no mechanism forces one temperature on all the ion populations. The failure was licensed by Module 1 and is observed here.

8.3 What is refuted, and what is not

Refuted: the transfer of a plane-interface, constant-acceleration, two-uniform-fluid, forgotten-seed mixing law to a decelerating supernova shell. Not refuted: the law itself, which Module 7 checked in the regime in which it was measured and which is not under test here.

Refuted: the transfer of a plane-interface, constant-acceleration, two-uniform-fluid, forgotten-seed mixing law to a decelerating supernova shell. Not refuted: the law itself, which Module 7 checked in the regime in which it was measured and which is not under test here.

$\alpha_B$ is the bubble coefficient. The observed quantity is a spike penetration — ejecta reaching outward into lighter gas — and at Atwood number near 1 spikes outrun bubbles, because a dense spike falling through a light fluid feels little drag while a light bubble rising through a dense one feels a great deal. The direction is certain. No number for $\alpha_{\rm spike}$ is printed anywhere in this module, because no paper this book holds gives one. That makes the $0.0073$ a lower bound on the prediction and the factor 11 an upper bound on the discrepancy.

The seed is not forgotten. The mixing law assumes the initial conditions are lost after about three merger generations — Module 7 quotes the assumption in the experimenters' own words. At a remnant's contact discontinuity the reverse shock feeds the interface continuously, and Wang & Chevalier find that reproducing Tycho's observed protrusions at all requires ejecta clumps with a density contrast of at least 100 over their surroundings. A structure that needs a seed of contrast 100 is not a structure that has forgotten its seed.

One fluid, one temperature. Refuted in §6.2 by the measurement itself. The electrons and the ions need not share a temperature, and at the termination shock a third population — pickup ions — takes 80 per cent of the energy. Module 1 supplies the criterion that says when this is allowed to happen; no module in this book carries a two-fluid or three-fluid shock.
The mixing law transferred from a plane interface. Refuted in §8 , by a factor 11, with the three reasons stated and no claim to have found the right law.

Module 3 put a star in hydrostatic balance and left it there. Module 2 derived the equation that governs what happens when the balance fails, and applied it to a flow whose radial structure was measured rather than predicted. This module does the thing neither of them did: it takes the steady spherical flow seriously as an equation to be solved, discovers that the equation has a singular point, and finds that almost everything worth knowing about stellar winds and about accretion onto compact objects follows from the behaviour of solutions near that point.

The singular point is the reason this is not a routine exercise. At one particular radius the coefficient of $\mathrm{d}v/\mathrm{d}r$ vanishes, and unless the right-hand side vanishes there too, the solution has infinite gradient and stops existing. That is a strong constraint, and §3 shows it selects exactly one value of an integration constant out of a continuum. The solution that satisfies it is the only one that starts subsonic at a stellar surface and ends supersonic at infinity — and a wind that does not end supersonic decelerates as $v \propto r^{-2}$, which is a qualitatively different object with a qualitatively different signature in the data. §7 uses exactly that: the sign of a measured velocity exponent separates the two, with no fitting.

The anchor is the solar wind , §7 . Venzmer & Bothmer (2018) fitted four power laws to the combined Helios 1 and 2 data between $0.29$ and $0.98$ au, each exponent fitted independently of the others and with no fluid equation imposed on the fit. Those four numbers confirm two predictions of this module and refute a third, and the sharpest of them is not a confirmation or a refutation at all but a measured shortfall: steady Euler, fed the measured pressure gradient and given no wind model whatever, accounts for about one third of the acceleration the wind is observed to have at 1 au. The same table was used in Module 2 §10 to confirm an exact conservation law and refute the adiabatic closure. §7.1 says in print what is new here and what is not, because a reader is entitled to ask whether the book is checking one table twice.

Three temperatures within the plausible range demand base densities spanning a factor of $186$. Given that the base density is itself an extrapolation below its source's fitted range ( §2.1 ), this comparison constrains very little, and saying so is more useful than quoting the one temperature at which the two happen to agree.

Proposition 5 needs three numbers: a mass, a gas density and a sound speed at the accretion radius. For the black hole at the centre of the Galaxy all three have been measured, which is rare, and a fourth quantity — the actual accretion rate — has been bounded independently, which is rarer. The comparison is therefore possible, and it is the largest ratio this book has produced.

The three comparisons of this section are statements about three different radii, and the figure exists so that they are not confused. The Bondi rate is computed from gas measured at $R_B$, five decades out. Marrone et al.'s limits come from Faraday rotation and depend on how far in the rotating medium extends: their upper limits assume an inner edge at 30–100 $r_S$, their lower limits at 3–10 $r_S$. The gas is expected to circularise near 100 $r_S$, which is where the first of Bondi's three premises fails. Nothing in the Bondi calculation knows that the region between $R_B$ and $r_S$ exists.
8.3 What is refuted, stated exactly

No outflow. Bondi's solution has $\dot M$ independent of radius by construction. The observed density profile near Sgr A* is shallower than the $r^{-3/2}$ that free-fall requires, which means $\dot M$ falls with decreasing radius: most of the gas captured at $R_B$ never arrives.

$r_S = 2GM/c^2 = 1.2699\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{cm} = 0.085$ au. With $R_B = 0.0811$ pc from §8 , $R_B/r_S = 1.970\times10^{5}$. The free-fall time from rest at $R_B$ is $t_{\rm ff} = (\pi/2)\sqrt{R_B^3/(2GM)} = 1.844\times10^{2}$ yr. The $\pi/2$ is what the substitution $r = R_B\cos^2\eta$ produces on integrating $\mathrm{d}r/\mathrm{d}t = -\sqrt{2GM(1/r - 1/R_B)}$, exactly as in Module 3 's free-fall calculation; the bare $\sqrt{R_B^3/(2GM)} = 117.4$ yr is the free-fall scale and not the time. Either figure is short enough that the flow has had ample time to reach a steady state, which is one premise of Proposition 5 that Sgr A* does not obviously violate.

With $\dot M = 9.843\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{g\,s^{-1}}$ and $v = 435.6\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$: $\tfrac12\dot Mv^2 = 9.3384\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, which is $2.440\times10^{-7}\,L_\odot$. The gravitational term $GM_\odot\dot M/R_\odot = 1.878\times10^{27}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}} = 4.91\times10^{-7}\,L_\odot$ — twice as large as the kinetic term , so most of the energy invested in the wind goes into lifting it out of the potential well rather than into its final speed. Verscharen et al.'s measured $F_E \approx 1$ au² g s⁻³ sr⁻¹ over the poles converts to $2.812\times10^{27}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}} = 7.35\times10^{-7}\,L_\odot$. The kinetic and gravitational terms sum to $2.81\times10^{27}$, and the agreement to three digits is a coincidence of a source figure quoted as "about $1$": the energy flux should exceed that sum by the enthalpy flux, $\tfrac52 c_T^2\dot M \approx 3.5\times10^{25}\ \mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$, about $1.3$ per cent, plus a conductive flux this module does not compute.

What it implies is that the calculation has refuted itself. A flow accreting three thousand times the Eddington rate would radiate far above $L_{\rm Edd}$, and the resulting radiation pressure would drive the gas away — violating the premise, used in Proposition 5, that radiation is dynamically unimportant. The honest reading is not "black holes in molecular clouds double in ten thousand years"; it is that spherical Bondi accretion is self-inconsistent in this regime, and a calculation that includes radiation is required. Module 13 supplies it.

A Reynolds number of $10^{9}$ in the layer of the Sun one can photograph is the fact this module exists to explain. It is not a number any laboratory reaches, and it is at the small end of the astrophysical range. What the rest of this section, and §3 , will show is that because it is so large, almost nothing about the flow can be computed — and that a surprising amount about it can nevertheless be predicted, with no calculation at all, from dimensions alone.

3. The dissipation scale, and what a simulation would cost

The inertial range of Definition 2 has a lower end, and the same counting that fixed the spectrum fixes where it is. This section builds that scale, and then uses it to price a direct numerical simulation — which is the calculation that decides, once and for all, that astrophysical turbulence is not going to be computed from first principles.

A softer count exists and it is wrong for this purpose, by a factor that can be named. Three quantities of a Keplerian disc, each divided by its own value at the inner radius. Two fall outward and one rises, and the one that rises is the one the Rayleigh criterion tests. The thin $\alpha$-disc captures a great deal for what it is: a one-parameter closure applied to a vertically averaged, axisymmetric, Keplerian flow. What it misses is a long list, and the interesting entries are the ones a shipped module of this book already asked for.

Ten modules of this book have written the same sentence in ten different ways: there is a magnetic field here, and it matters, and we are not carrying it. Module 1 ended with a plasma whose mean free path exceeds the system size and could say only that a field must be doing the confining. Module 2 left the intracluster medium with a Reynolds number of about $600$ and a thermal conduction problem it handed on without a number. Module 5 could not say what holds a subcritical cloud up. Module 7 needed a statement accurate to one degree about a field its source never measured. Module 10 confirmed Kolmogorov's exponent most cleanly on a magnetic spectrum in a plasma its own argument does not describe. Twenty such promises are on the record, each with the file and line it was printed at, and this module exists to pay them.

What it costs is small, and that is the surprise. One term is added to Module 2 's momentum equation — the Lorentz force — and one equation is added to close it, which is Ohm's law fed into Faraday's. Nothing else changes. Module 2 §4 proved its moment hierarchy under the hypothesis $\nabla_{\mathbf v}\cdot\mathbf a = 0$, and observed in the same breath that the Lorentz force $\mathbf a = (q/mc)\,\mathbf v\times\mathbf B$ satisfies it, so that "Magnetohydrodynamics, in Module 12, therefore inherits (4.1) unchanged". The result of Proposition 4 is Alfvén's, in a one-page note of 1942. That paper was not fetched for this book and is cited for the result only , in the same way Module 1 cites Maxwell (1867); its volume, pages and date were confirmed at Crossref and nothing else about it is claimed here. The proof above is this module's own.

Module 7 §9.5 states the debt in one line: "A purely hydrodynamic calculation that needs a one-degree statement about a field it never mentions is a calculation waiting for magnetohydrodynamics." Its Proposition 9 says that Kelvin–Helmholtz growth at the observed rate requires $$ B\cos\theta \;\lt \; \Delta U\sqrt{\frac{2\pi\rho_h\rho_l}{\rho_h+\rho_l}} \tag{4.2}$$ for equal fields on both sides of the interface, with $4\pi$ in place of $2\pi$ if the field is one-sided. That inequality is recomputed here from Proposition 6's dispersion relation rather than copied, so that the comparison below is able to fail.

And here is the gap this module cannot fill. The book's shape is: derive the terrestrial result, change the regime, check against a measured astronomical number. Module 4 had the speed of sound in air, Module 6 the dry adiabat, Module 10 the Kolmogorov constant. Magnetohydrodynamics has terrestrial measurements — Alfvén waves were first seen in liquid mercury, and every tokamak is an MHD experiment — and none of them was read for this book. What occupies the terrestrial slot above is a reproduction of Module 7 , which is a check against this book and not against a laboratory. The four checks of §§5 – 8 are all astronomical, and a reader should weigh them knowing that no bench-top number stands behind them.

Close to the Sun the field is strong and the wind slow, so $v \lt v_{\rm A}$ and the field controls the flow: it can enforce corotation, and it carries away angular momentum. Far out the wind is fast and the field weak, so $v \gt v_{\rm A}$ and the flow drags the field, which is what §5 just measured. In between there is a surface where the two are equal, and it is the boundary between those two regimes.

Module 1 §8 observed that the magnetic rescue of the fluid description is partial, and partial in a measurable way. A field constrains motion across itself and does nothing to motion along itself, so a magnetised collisionless plasma is not an ordinary fluid with a scalar pressure: it has $p_\parallel$ along the field and $p_\perp$ across it, and the two relax toward each other only through collisions the plasma is not having. The resulting description is the Chew–Goldberger–Low or double-adiabatic theory. Pressure anisotropy is routinely measured in the solar wind, and it drives the firehose and mirror instabilities, which scatter particles and so act as the plasma's substitute for collisions.

Photons carry momentum, and a fluid that is lit from inside feels it. This module derives the Eddington limit that five shipped pages have been quoting, prices the composition hidden in its proton mass, and evaluates the one computation the book deferred by name. Four checks: one reproduction confirmed, a column-mean opacity confirmed to a factor of 1.1482, one refutation of the adiabatic assumption at the photosphere, and a grey atmosphere that holds to three per cent.

The factor $3$ in $t_{\rm diff}$ is the $1/3$ of Proposition 4, and it is the same $1/3$ as in Module 1 §6 's kinetic-theory transport coefficients, $\mu \simeq \tfrac13\rho v\lambda$ ( module01.html:363 ): a flux carried by carriers of speed $v$ and free path $\lambda$ has diffusivity $\tfrac13 v\lambda$, and for photons $v = c$. Proposition 3's random walk had no such factor, because it did not fix the geometry; this is the factor it set aside. The step-1 version of this module's generator carried the $3$ as "the standard three-dimensional correction", with no source; Gate D ruled that it be derived rather than sourced, and it is derived here.

What is refuted is the reading of (6.1) as a local opacity, and Fig. 2 shows why. The inference averages $\kappa_{\rm R}$ over the whole column from $\tau_{\rm R} = 0$ to $2/3$, across which ATLAS9's $\kappa_{\rm R}$ rises by a factor of $10.48$ from $\tau_{\rm R} = 0.01$. It keeps rising below: from $0.3596$ at $\tau_{\rm R} = 0.543$ to $0.7274$ at $1$, a factor of $2.0228$ in $32.6$ km. A column mean cannot be recovered as a local value when the opacity changes that fast. §7 needs the local value, and that is why it takes $\kappa_{\rm R}$ from ATLAS9 and not from (6.1).

Eddington did not state a limiting luminosity, and he did not use electron scattering. In his Sect. 82, p. 115, of The Internal Constitution of the Stars he derives "an upper limit to the opacity $k$ in any star (perfect gas or not) for which $L$ and $M$ are known by observation", and gives its physical reading on the same page: "the radiation observed to be emitted must work its way through the star, and if there were too much obstruction it would blow up the star".

The limit's assumptions, each of which can fail. It assumes spherical symmetry, so that the flux at $r$ is $L/4\pi r^2$; a disc or a beam puts the flux where the gas is not. It assumes the opacity is electron scattering; any additional absorption lowers $L_{\rm Edd}$. And it assumes a steady state; a transient can exceed it while it blows the gas away. This module names no observed violation, because none was read.

Four systems on one logarithmic axis of $L/L_{\rm Edd}$. Two kinds of point. Filled circles are measured luminosities over the Eddington luminosity: Sgr A*'s X-ray luminosity at $3.70\times10^{-12}$ and the Sun at $2.6772\times10^{-5}$ (with $\kappa_{\rm es}$ at $X = 0.7583$). Open diamonds are accretion rates over $\dot M_{\rm Edd}$, which equal $L/L_{\rm Edd}$ only if the gas radiates at $\eta_{\rm rad} = 0.1$: Module 11's AGN disc at $0.100002$ and Module 9's Bondi hole at $3663.5$ (printed there as $3664$). The Bondi hole lies above the line at $1$, which is Module 9's self-inconsistency drawn as a point.

Every astrophysical simulation solves a problem that is not the one written down, and this module says which one. It derives the Courant condition that Module 10 used, the viscosity that every grid code adds to the equations it solves, and the exact Riemann solver on which Godunov's method is built. It then runs three one-dimensional codes against closed forms that this book already owns. Four checks: a stability boundary reproduced, a convergence rate predicted with no fitted parameter, a blast wave in the right place with its peak too low, and a particle method whose error at a contact does not decrease with resolution.

What this does to Module 10's count. Module 10 Proposition 4 took the step of a simulation as $\delta t \sim \eta/U$: one smallest cell, crossed at the flow speed. For an explicit code that solves the compressible equations, the signal speed in Definition 1 is $|u| + c_{\rm s}$, and the step is $\Delta x/(U + c_{\rm s})$. That takes $1 + 1/M$ times as many steps, with $M = U/c_{\rm s}$ the Mach number. For Module 10's laboratory air, the thermal Mach number $U/\bar v = 0.0218$ ( module10.html:148 ) and $c_{\rm s}/\bar v = (\pi\gamma/8)^{1/2} = 0.7415$ at $\gamma = 1.4$ give $M = 0.0294$ and a factor of $35.01$. For the supersonic cloud of Module 10 §6 , $U = 2.64\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ against $c_{\rm s} = 0.2439\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$ gives $M = 10.825$ and a factor of $1.0924$. Module 10's $\delta t \sim \eta/U$ is the step of a code that has removed sound waves, which is what an incompressible code does. It is right to within $9.24$ per cent for the cloud, and it undercounts a compressible code's work on the wind tunnel by a factor of $35.01$. Module 10 is not changed. Its $\mathrm{Re}^{3}$ counts the steps of a code without sound waves, so for a compressible explicit code it is a lower bound on the work, short by the factor $1 + 1/M$. Module 10 calls only its snapshot column a floor ( module10.html:283 ); this result shows that its work column is one too.

The run advects a Gaussian 200 steps on 400 cells at $C = 0.25$, $0.5$ and $0.9$ and finds the ratio of measured to predicted variance growth to be $1.000000000$ each time. A code that runs at a flow speed $U$ on $N$ cells across a length $L$ therefore has a numerical Reynolds number $$ \mathrm{Re}_{\rm num} \;=\; \frac{UL}{D_{\rm num}} \;=\; \frac{2N}{1 - C}. \tag{3.3}$$ At $N = 1024$ this is $4096$ at $C = 0.5$ and $2.048\times10^{4}$ at $C = 0.9$. That is the answer to module10.html:285 for the upwind scheme: the code solves Euler's equations plus a viscosity that the grid sets, and the Reynolds number it runs at is a property of $N$ and $C$ and not of the gas. Better schemes than upwind reduce $D_{\rm num}$ in smooth flow, and §10 gives the bound that holds for any scheme.
11. Which numbers in this book came from a simulation

The plan of this book asked this module to say which of its results came from a simulation and which from a closed form. Two readers went through Modules 1 to 13 and classified every number that a module compares against or takes as an input: (a) the output of a numerical simulation; (b) a numerical model built by solving equations on a computer, such as the BS05 solar model table or the ATLAS9 model atmosphere; (c) an ordinary differential equation with no closed form, integrated numerically, by this book's own script or, in 3 of the 30 rows, by a published integration (Chandrasekhar's in Module 3, Kandori's in Module 5), such as Lane–Emden, Bonnor–Ebert, Sedov, or the critical solutions of Bondi and Parker. The count is by table row, and one row can hold several numbers from one source.
modules (a) simulation (b) numerical model (c) an ODE with no closed form, integrated numerically

The closed-form results that carry the book are the other column: the mean free paths of Module 1 , the jump conditions and the $2/5$ exponent of Module 8 , Kolmogorov's $5/3$ and $4/5$ in Module 10 , the Eddington limit of Module 13 . Class (c) is not simulation in the sense of this module: it is a quadrature whose error the book controls and reports, as Module 8 §4 does for $\xi_0$ to eight digits. Classes (a) and (b) are inputs whose error the book does not control.
